title: Maximal tori give sections of the solvable torus quotient
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness, connectedness and morphism properties have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-pc-morphism-conventions]. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. A smooth group is unipotent if every geometric point is a unipotent matrix in a faithful linear representation, meaning $(u-I)^n=0$ for some $n\geq1$. A torus is a group isomorphic over $F$ to $\mathbf G_m^r$, where $r\geq0$ and $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ for a commutative $F$-algebra $A$; a maximal torus is a torus subgroup maximal under inclusion. Let $H$ be smooth, connected and solvable. Let $U\subseteq H$ be a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup such that the fppf sheaf quotient $D=H/U$ is a torus; here fppf sheaf quotient means sheafification of $A\mapsto H(A)/U(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. For every maximal torus $T\subseteq H$, the restriction $q|_T:T\to D$ of the quotient homomorphism is an isomorphism of group schemes.

source.place: Theorems 16.26(a) and 16.27(b), pp.332--333; Theorem 16.33(d), pp.335--336, identifies maximal diagonalizable complements as maximal tori when D is a torus.

proof.text: The successive commutator subgroups give a finite normal series with commutative quotients, so the solvability hypothesis is the one used in [lem-sfb-lie-kolchin-triangular-embedding]. Apply that node over $F$ to embed $H$ as a closed subgroup of $B_n$. Write $V=H\cap U_n$. By [lem-sfb-triangular-diagonal-kernel], the quotient $q_0:H\to D_0=H/V$ has $V$ unipotent, a closed embedding of $D_0$ into a split torus, and a group-scheme section $s_0:D_0\to H$. In particular $D_0$ is of multiplicative type in the sense used by [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial].

source.place: Theorem 16.30, printed pp.334–335; Theorem 16.21, p.330; Theorem 16.26(a), pp.332–333.

proof.text: Identify $U$ with $V$ before using the section. The smooth geometric-point notion of unipotence for $U$ agrees with the scheme-theoretic notion by [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial]. That node makes $q_0|_U:U\to D_0$ trivial, so $U\subseteq\ker q_0=V$. It also makes $q|_V:V\to D$ trivial, since $V$ is scheme-theoretically unipotent and $D$ is a torus, so $V\subseteq\ker q=U$; the kernel identification for $q$ is [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. These are inclusions of subgroup functors on all algebras, hence $U=V$ as subgroup schemes. Both $D_0$ and $D$ represent the same sheaf quotient $H/U$; its universal property identifies them compatibly with the quotient maps. Transport $s_0$ to a group-scheme section $s:D\to H$ with $q s=\operatorname{id}_D$.

source.place: Theorem 16.21, printed p.330, identification of the largest unipotent subgroup; Corollary 14.18(a), p.284; quotient interpretation in Section 5(j), pp.116–118.

proof.text: Let $T\subseteq H$ be the given maximal torus and set $K=T\cap U$. Since $U=H\cap U_n$, the group $K$ is a closed subgroup of $U_n$, hence is unipotent by the unitriangular definition. Apply [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial] to the inclusion $K\to T$; it is trivial on every algebra, so $K$ is the trivial group scheme. Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] to $q|_T$. Its kernel is $K=1$, and it factors as $T\to S\hookrightarrow D$, with $S$ representing the fppf quotient $T/1$. This quotient sheaf is $T$ itself: dividing each $T(A)$ by the trivial subgroup changes nothing. Thus the induced $a:T\xrightarrow{\sim}S$ is an isomorphism of group schemes, not merely a bijection on $F$-points. In particular $S$ is a torus and a closed subgroup of $D$.

source.place: Theorem 16.27(b), printed p.333, first paragraph of its proof; Homomorphism Theorem 5.39, p.108.

proof.text: Form $P=H\times_D S$, the inverse image of $S$. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], $P/U\simeq S$ as fppf quotient, with the restricted quotient map. The group $P$ is a closed subgroup of the same $B_n$, and $P\cap U_n=U$: it contains $U$ and is contained in $H$. There are two sections of $P\to S$, namely $s|_S$ and the inclusion $T\hookrightarrow P$ composed with $a^{-1}:S\to T$. Here $S$ is smooth because $a:T\xrightarrow{\sim}S$ identifies it with a torus; also $P$ is smooth and connected by the same quotient node, since $U$ and $S$ are smooth and connected. Apply [lem-sfb-triangular-quotient-section-conjugacy] with $J=P$, $V=U$ and smooth quotient $S$ to these sections. It gives $u\in U(F)$ such that $T=\operatorname{Int}(u)s(S)$ as subgroup schemes of $H$. Thus $T\subseteq\operatorname{Int}(u)s(D)$.

source.place: Theorem 16.27(a),(b), printed p.333, inverse-image subgroup and comparison of its two sections, with the smooth quotient hypothesis retained as in Summary 16.29(b), printed p.334.

proof.text: Put $b=\operatorname{Int}(u)\circ s:D\to H$. Since $q(u)=1$, for every algebra $A$ the equality $q_A(u_A s_A(d)u_A^{-1})=d$ shows $q b=\operatorname{id}_D$. Consequently $\ker b=1$. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization], $b$ identifies $D$ with a closed subgroup $T'$ of $H$ (its fppf image is $D/1=D$). This is a torus containing $T$ by the preceding step. Maximality gives $T=T'$. On this subgroup $q b=\operatorname{id}_D$ and $b q=\operatorname{id}_{T'}$, so $q|_T$ is an isomorphism, as required.

source.place: Theorem 16.27(b), printed p.333, maximality conclusion; Theorem 16.33(d), p.336.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 16.27(b), printed p.333, with Theorems 16.26(a), 16.30 and the quotient identification of Theorem 16.21. The proof constructs the containing section torus and invokes maximality.
